title: Compact Signal Coordinator and Soft Evict Protocol for Interleaved KV
creator: Maya Chen
description: Multiplexed serving workloads are causing frequent KV fragmentation and eviction churn in paged attention. Existing heuristics either over-evict (hurting reuse) or under-evict (increasing memory pressure and tail latencies). This ticket introduces two coordinated pieces: (1) a Compact Signal Coordinator (CSC) that aggregates lightweight residency and touch-pattern signals across shards and microblocks to surface compactability candidates, and (2) a Soft Evict Protocol (SEP) that applies staged, reversible eviction steps with admission gating to avoid decode/prefill stalls. Together these aim to reduce fragmentation-induced decode amplification, lower tail latency, and improve KV reuse for interleaved inference patterns.
acceptance_criteria: CSC computes a compactability score per microblock and exposes a streaming metric for the scheduler
SEP reduces eviction-induced prefill stalls by >= 30% on the multiplexed test harness compared to baseline
End-to-end median and 95th decode latency do not regress more than 5% under nominal load
A/B dashboard available showing hit-rate, eviction rate, and compacted-bytes over time
Design doc and implementation reviewed by Storage and Inference runtime leads
technical_design: At runtime the CSC runs as a lightweight aggregator colocated with KV shards. It maintains aggregated touch histograms (temporal buckets), interleaving density metrics (how many distinct requests touch a segment within a time window), and a compactability score that combines coldness, fragmentation ratio, and decode-cost delta if compacted. The SEP introduces a two-phase eviction: a soft-mark phase that marks candidates and reduces admission score for incoming prefill, and a conditional-freeze phase that starts background compaction if the segment remains cold. The SEP uses token-cost-aware thresholds: segments with high expected decode-cost (based on KV size and access frequency) are preferentially compacted rather than immediately evicted. Integration points: kernel scheduler consults CSC signals when choosing kernel batch composition; prefill admission rejects or throttles feeds to segments in soft-mark with exponential backoff; background compactor runs with IO and decode budgets to avoid impacting latency SLOs.
implementation_plan: Prototype CSC signal aggregator as an opt-in module behind runtime flag
Add compactability score computation and metric export (Prometheus)
Implement SEP soft-mark state machine with reversible marks stored in shard metadata
Wire scheduler and prefill admission to consult CSC/SEP signals (non-blocking calls)
Add background compactor with configurable budgets and safepoints
Run microbench harness with multiplexed interleaved traces and iterate thresholds
Roll out canary in dedicated capacity pool, monitor dashboards, and progressively expand
testing_plan: Unit tests for CSC aggregation and score computation (deterministic inputs)
Integration test: simulate 1000 concurrent short-lived requests to reproduce fragmentation pattern
Load test: compare baseline vs CSC+SEP under synthetic multiplexed traffic (latency, hit-rate)
Chaos test: kill compactor mid-compact and verify SEP reversibility and consistency
Regression test: ensure no increased tail latencies on long-sequence generation workloads
risks_mitigation: Risk: CSC misclassifies hot segments as compactable -> Mitigation: conservative thresholds and quick undo path
Risk: Background compaction competes with decoder kernels -> Mitigation: compactor runs with strict GPU/CPU budgets and off-peak scheduling
Risk: New metrics overload observability -> Mitigation: sample signals and aggregate histograms before export
Risk: Cross-tenant interference in shared pools -> Mitigation: tenant-aware scoring and quota isolation in SEP

decisions: Store CSC soft-mark as a compact per-microblock byte to minimize metadata churn
Use a combined compactability score (coldness + fragmentation + expected decode cost) rather than single-metric thresholds
Prefer compaction over hard-eviction when expected decode-cost savings justify background work
Expose sampling of CSC signals rather than full streaming to limit observability costs
